heading: PROPHET ZAKARIYYĀ (AS)
title: THE QUIET PRAYER AND THE LEGACY OF GOODNESS
themes: Tawḥīd • Sincere Duʿāʾ • Hope • Guardianship • Gratitude • Remembrance • Humility • Doing Good
scope: 8 CONNECTED STORIES | 12 INTERACTIVE MISSIONS | 17 SELECTED QUR’ANIC VERSES
introduction: Volume Twenty-Two follows the ʿIBRAH Junior journey after Prophet Yūnus (AS) and focuses on Prophet Zakariyyā (peace be upon him). The Qur’an honours Zakariyyā as a righteous Prophet (al-Anʿām 6:85) and recounts his guardianship of Maryam, his heartfelt private supplication, the glad tidings of Yaḥyā, the distinctive sign Allah granted him, and his household’s eagerness in doing good. The principal passages are Āl ʿImrān 3:37–41, Maryam 19:2–11 and al-Anbiyāʾ 21:89–90. The full account must be read through these revealed texts; the manuscript does not invent a historical childhood, household conversation, precise age, location, occupation, dates or death account.

The fictional modern continuity begins with Imaan, Akhlaq, their parents Salaam and Salamah, Dadi Jaan, Sheikh Uncle, Sir Zameer, Mohsin and Mohsina preparing a “Quiet Hope, Lasting Goodness” school exhibition. Their contemporary conversations are imagined teaching applications. They neither witness Zakariyyā’s life nor become him in games. The sacred glad tidings concern a particular Prophet and cannot be turned into a guarantee about pregnancy, family structure, delayed wishes or every individual duʿāʾ.

stories.title: The Folder with the Missing Word
stories.subtitle: The next Prophet and the value of accurate learning

blocks.text: The academy exhibition about Prophet Yūnus (AS) had ended, but one corner of Sheikh Uncle’s library remained filled with coloured folders. Imaan was stacking them by volume while Akhlaq guarded a tiny cardboard compass. It had never really led them anywhere, yet he liked to imagine it could point to the next lesson.

“Look!” he said. “One folder has no title.” The emerald cover contained a single line: A PRAYER THAT WAS HEARD EVEN WHEN SPOKEN QUIETLY. The rest of the page was blank. Mohsin guessed that it was a mystery story. Mohsina thought it might be a poem. Akhlaq suggested adding a dramatic picture of a Prophet standing on a mountain.

“Before anyone draws,” Sheikh Uncle said, “we must discover what the Qur’an actually tells us.” He opened Sūrah Maryam and read its opening mention of Allah’s mercy toward His servant Zakariyyā. He explained that Zakariyyā was a Prophet and that the Qur’an gives us true episodes of his devotion, prayer and Allah’s kindness. “We will not invent where he stood, what he wore or how his face looked,” he added.

Imaan wrote ZAKARIYYĀ beneath the verse reference. She wanted to add a date and a map, but neither could be established from the passage. Instead she wrote SOURCE FIRST. Akhlaq looked disappointed. “Is a story exciting if we cannot fill in every empty space?”
Dadi Jaan, who had come to take them home, smiled. “A beautiful account does not need our guesses to make it important. Think of how much there is to understand in one truthful prayer.”

At dinner Salaam asked whether the children had enjoyed discovering the new subject. “Yes,” Akhlaq answered, “but I almost gave Zakariyyā a made-up mountain.” Everyone laughed gently. He corrected himself before anyone else could: “I learned that respect means leaving out what we do not know.”
On the folder Imaan added a second sentence: A GREAT STORY CAN BEGIN WITH A QUIET VOICE. The compass stayed on the shelf. The next direction had come from the Qur’an.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour the revealed account by checking the source and leaving unsupported details aside.

stories.title: A Prayer No One Needed to Hear
stories.subtitle: Quiet duʿāʾ, personal dignity and trust

blocks.text: The morning after the new folder appeared, Imaan found Akhlaq sitting by the window with a notebook closed against his knees. Usually he would announce his plans before breakfast. Today he was thoughtful.

“Are you worried about something?” Imaan asked. Akhlaq hesitated. There was a school responsibility he wanted to manage well, but he did not feel ready to explain it to everyone. “I’d like to make duʿāʾ,” he replied, “without turning it into a class discussion.”

Salamah heard the exchange and welcomed both thoughts. “Allah hears us even when we speak quietly,” she said. “You may talk to Him in duʿāʾ. And if you ever need help with something unsafe or troubling, you can speak to us or another trustworthy adult. Privacy is not the same as keeping dangerous secrets.”

That afternoon Sheikh Uncle read Sūrah Maryam 19:3: Zakariyyā called on his Lord privately. He explained that this was a real Qur’anic account, not a rule that a child must always pray silently or hide difficulties. A person may ask Allah openly or quietly and may also seek appropriate support.

Sir Zameer then offered a modern challenge. Every group had to design a way for pupils to request classroom help without announcing private worries to their peers. Mohsina suggested a discreet message box checked by a teacher. Mohsin wanted everyone to write their requests on a public board so that the class could choose which deserved help.

Imaan pointed out the problem. “Nobody should have to share a private matter in front of everyone just to be heard.” The group designed a short form with three options: I NEED HELP WITH LEARNING, I NEED TO SPEAK TO AN ADULT, and I WOULD LIKE A PRIVATE CONVERSATION. It also reminded children to tell an adult straight away about danger.
When the form was tested, a younger pupil used it to ask for a quieter seat during reading. The teacher listened and made a simple change without making the child the subject of a class announcement.

That evening Akhlaq opened his notebook. He had completed the responsibility that worried him by asking his father for guidance and taking one step at a time. He wrote: I CAN MAKE DUʿĀʾ, AND I CAN ASK FOR HELP. Neither kindness nor trust demanded a performance in front of an audience.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Make duʿāʾ sincerely and seek trusted help when it is needed.

Sir Zameer announced that a younger class would start using the academy reading corner. Team Amanah had to prepare the space so children of different heights and reading abilities could enjoy it. Mohsin brought a box of books. Mohsina counted the cushions. Imaan checked the reading labels, while Akhlaq rushed toward the highest shelf.
“This corner will be perfect!” he said, reaching for a large picture book. “I’ll put all the best books right at the top so they look impressive.”

“Would the younger children be able to reach them?” Mohsina asked. Akhlaq paused. He had been imagining what adults would praise, not what the younger children needed. The group moved favourite books down and left space for a child using a walking aid.

Sheikh Uncle visited with a Qur’an opened to Āl ʿImrān 3:37. He explained that Allah placed Maryam in the care of Zakariyyā, and that the passage also tells of provision Maryam received by Allah’s will. “This account honours a real relationship of care,” he said. “We cannot retell it with invented domestic conversations. Our modern lesson is much smaller: when you are entrusted with someone’s wellbeing, think of their actual needs.”

Akhlaq asked whether looking after someone means deciding everything for them. “No,” Salamah replied later. “Responsible care must protect dignity, not treat a person as a project.” The team asked younger pupils which kinds of books they wanted. One preferred short sentences. Another enjoyed animals. A third wanted to sit close enough to see the illustrations.

The children had also received a donation of crayons. Mohsin suggested declaring that the donation was evidence the team would now always get whatever it asked for. Imaan shook her head. “We should thank Allah and the donor. We cannot promise that every request will be answered in this exact way.”

The first reading session was noisy and cheerful. Several books were borrowed; two cushions slipped out of place; the class asked for clearer signs. Instead of defending their design, Team Amanah made small improvements.

That night Akhlaq wrote under the lesson: A GIFT CALLS FOR GRATITUDE. A TRUST CALLS FOR CARE. The compass lay nearby, pointing nowhere in particular, but the new reading corner had become a place where children truly felt included.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Responsible care notices real needs and responds with gratitude.

stories.title: The Questions We Can Ask Kindly
stories.subtitle: Hope, respectful questions and concern for guidance

blocks.text: A folded letter arrived for Sheikh Uncle’s Academy. A former pupil had written to thank the teachers for helping him love reading when he was younger. He now taught younger students in his neighbourhood. Sir Zameer showed the letter to Team Amanah, who were designing a display about what people pass on to others.

“We should make a wall of famous families,” Mohsin said. “That will look important.” Imaan thought of the previous volumes about Ibrāhīm, Isḥāq and Yaʿqūb. “Those were Prophets,” she answered. “The Qur’an honoured them for guidance from Allah, not for winning a popularity contest. Maybe our wall should show how good teaching can continue.”

Dadi Jaan came for the Qur’an discussion. She read from Sūrah Maryam 19:4–6, explaining that Zakariyyā spoke of his old age, expressed concern for what would follow him, and asked Allah for a successor who would be pleasing to Him. Some precise meanings in the passage require classical Tafsīr; children should not reduce it to a contest over possessions.
Akhlaq raised his hand. “May we ask questions about the verse?”
“Of course,” Dadi said. “Respectful questions help us understand. But we should never use someone’s age or family situation as a joke. Zakariyyā’s prayer was sincere and worthy of respect.”

Later a younger child asked why the school’s oldest volunteer still came to arrange the books. Akhlaq nearly answered, “Because he has nothing better to do.” He caught himself. That sentence would have been unkind and untrue. Instead he helped the child ask the volunteer directly what he enjoyed about serving.
The volunteer smiled. “I like seeing young readers discover something useful. Somebody helped me when I was learning.” He showed them how to repair a worn book cover without tearing the pages.

The class made a display called GOODNESS WE CAN PASS ON. Each leaf named a voluntary action: teach carefully, care for books, tell the truth, listen to elders, share useful knowledge. Nobody had to name private family struggles or prove a perfect home.

At home Akhlaq understood why the letter from the former pupil mattered. Not every lasting gift could be held in the hand. Knowledge, gentleness and service could continue in the lives of people we helped.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Respectful questions and useful teaching can make goodness continue.

stories.title: A Name Written with Gratitude
stories.subtitle: Good news and appreciating blessings without false promises

blocks.text: The academy was preparing welcome packets for pupils joining midterm. Mohsina had made bright name cards, and Akhlaq was responsible for spelling each name correctly. In his hurry he wrote YAHYA on an exhibition card beside Zakariyyā, then turned it over to add decorations.
“You remembered the name,” Imaan said. “But can you explain why it belongs in our lesson?”

At the afternoon session, Sheikh Uncle read Maryam 19:7 and Āl ʿImrān 3:39. The Qur’an records the special glad tidings of a son named Yaḥyā, who would be a Prophet among the righteous. This news was given by Allah to Zakariyyā; the children were not to imagine hearing angels themselves or reenact the moment.

“What if a family has been waiting and never receives the same kind of news?” Mohsin asked. The room became quiet. Sheikh Uncle answered carefully. “This particular gift tells us of Allah’s power and mercy in a specific event. We may hope, make duʿāʾ and offer kindness. We must never promise another family an identical outcome or judge anyone’s faith by their circumstances.”

Akhlaq remembered a card he had written for a new pupil. It said, YOUR FIRST DAY WILL BE AMAZING, EVERYONE WILL LOVE YOU, AND NOTHING WILL GO WRONG. He realised how much he had promised without knowing the future.
Together the children rewrote the card: WE ARE GLAD YOU ARE HERE. WE WILL HELP YOU FIND YOUR CLASS AND JOIN OUR GAMES. Each sentence described something they could actually try to do.

The following morning one new pupil became nervous in the corridor and wanted to sit quietly instead of joining a group activity. Team Amanah respected that wish. Imaan showed the timetable. Mohsina asked whether the pupil needed the teacher. Akhlaq offered a book without demanding a smile.
When they returned to the exhibition, Mohsin said, “So the lesson is that blessings should make us grateful, not boastful or careless.”
Akhlaq wrote Yaḥyā’s name carefully in the source folder and added a small note underneath: WE HONOUR THE NEWS ALLAH GAVE; WE DO NOT CLAIM TO KNOW EVERYONE’S FUTURE.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Celebrate blessings without guaranteeing outcomes only Allah knows.

stories.title: The Message Without a Voice
stories.subtitle: A particular Qur’anic sign and accessible communication

blocks.text: During a school presentation rehearsal, Akhlaq tried to speak while carrying three folders and pointing at a poster. Nobody understood which table he meant. He repeated himself more loudly, but the confusion grew. Mohsina finally set down her notebook and asked him to show the correct place with a clear arrow.

That afternoon Sir Zameer read Maryam 19:10–11 and Āl ʿImrān 3:41. Allah gave Zakariyyā a particular sign involving an inability to speak to people for the stated period; Zakariyyā then signalled his people to glorify Allah morning and evening. This was a sign from Allah in sacred history, not a game, a challenge to imitate or an explanation for ordinary communication difficulties.

Akhlaq suggested that everyone should have a contest to remain silent for three days. Sir Zameer stopped that plan at once. “We must not copy this unique sign,” he said. “And no child should be prevented from speaking, asking for help or expressing discomfort. We can learn a separate, respectful lesson about communicating clearly and making school activities accessible.”

The teacher introduced a visitor who used a communication board and gestures as well as speech. With permission, the visitor demonstrated how people may communicate differently. Team Amanah practised asking before helping, giving enough time for answers, and listening without impatience. No one pretended to be unable to speak.

For the exhibition Akhlaq drew three ordinary signs: HELP PLEASE, THANK YOU and THIS WAY. He checked that the pictures were clear and the words readable. Mohsina added a note explaining that gestures and communication aids are useful tools, not reasons to treat anyone as less capable.

When a younger pupil later pointed to a sign instead of interrupting a reading session, Akhlaq understood how much thought a small design could contain. He made room on the noticeboard for larger type and a written version of the announcements.

At home Dadi Jaan asked him what he had learned about Zakariyyā’s sign. “That Allah gave him a particular sign,” Akhlaq replied, “and that we should report it truthfully. Our school activity is about respecting how people communicate—not reenacting his miracle.”
He added a card to his folder: LISTEN WITH PATIENCE. HELP WITHOUT ASSUMING.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Honour a specific Qur’anic sign while supporting real-world communication needs.

The academy’s activity board had become crowded with projects, reminders and coloured labels. Imaan noticed that everyone was eager to begin new things, but several small responsibilities were forgotten as soon as the excitement faded. The reading corner needed tidying; donated books had to be returned; the class plants needed someone to check them.

Sir Zameer asked Team Amanah to design a simple routine that did not depend on prizes or public competitions. “Could we begin with one useful act each morning and finish with one moment of gratitude?” Imaan suggested.

At the Qur’an lesson, Dadi Jaan read Maryam 19:11 and Āl ʿImrān 3:41. The verses tell of Zakariyyā directing his people to glorify Allah morning and evening, and of Allah’s command to remember Him much. “These are words of worship,” she said. “They are not a stopwatch challenge. We should learn appropriate dhikr with understanding, gently and consistently.”

Mohsin proposed a huge points chart with names ranked from most religious to least religious. Salamah explained why that would be unfair. “Children have different abilities, family routines and private circumstances. We cannot score their hearts, or make them prove worship publicly.”

The team prepared optional personal cards instead. Each card held two simple prompts: IN THE MORNING, REMEMBER ALLAH AND CHOOSE A KIND ACTION. IN THE EVENING, THANK ALLAH AND NOTICE WHAT CAN IMPROVE. No one had to submit photographs, recordings or private answers.

Akhlaq tried the routine for one day. Before school he made a short duʿāʾ and helped lay out breakfast cups. After Maghrib he remembered the class plants and asked his father how to care for them the next day. He had not completed every task, but he did not treat that as a reason to abandon the routine.

The following afternoon Mohsina returned a book somebody had mistakenly placed in her bag. Mohsin corrected a label without announcing his kindness. Imaan helped the youngest group find their reading sheets. Small actions had begun to feel less like a performance and more like part of daily life.
Dadi asked what they would carry forward. Akhlaq answered, “Remember Allah often. Then make sure our hands are doing something good as well.”

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Remember Allah often and practise consistent, voluntary good deeds.

The final day of the “Quiet Hope, Lasting Goodness” exhibition arrived. Team Amanah had built eight stations, each with an accurate Qur’anic reference and a separate, clearly labelled modern example. No one had drawn Prophets, invented conversations, or turned a sacred sign into a challenge. The emerald folder was almost full.

At the entrance stood an empty branch made from paper. Under it Imaan had written: WHAT SHOULD CONTINUE AFTER THIS EXHIBITION? Visitors could choose one ordinary action that might benefit somebody else. A little girl chose helping a younger brother pack schoolbooks. A father chose to read with his children more regularly. A teacher chose to listen without interrupting.

Sheikh Uncle invited the family to hear al-Anbiyāʾ 21:89–90. Zakariyyā called upon Allah. Allah granted him Yaḥyā and described the family as eager in good deeds, turning to Allah in hope and reverent fear, and humble before Him. Salaam explained that their special gift belonged to Allah’s wisdom, while their qualities of worship and goodness offered powerful guidance.
Mohsin pointed to the branch. “Can we award the best person a golden leaf?”
“No,” Imaan replied. “We can celebrate good actions, but we cannot decide whose heart is best before Allah. The leaf should be a reminder, not a prize for spiritual rank.”

An elderly neighbour approached the display and read the cards slowly. She said she had been glad to see the children speak respectfully about people who hoped for things they could not control. Akhlaq wanted to ask about her personal life, but Dadi caught his eye. The children simply offered her a chair and showed her the part about making duʿāʾ with hope.

As the gathering ended, Sir Zameer asked the children to name the most lasting part of Zakariyyā’s story. Akhlaq first said, “A son named Yaḥyā.” Then he thought again. “That was the extraordinary blessing,” he replied. “But the Qur’an also shows us sincere prayer, humble worship and eagerness to do good.”
Imaan placed the final leaf on the paper branch: KINDNESS DOES NOT NEED AN AUDIENCE.
Dadi Jaan handed them a new, unopened blue folder. On its cover appeared a single name: YAḤYĀ. “The next world will teach us more about the son whom Allah honoured,” she said.
The compass still did not glow. Akhlaq no longer expected it to. He had learned that the clearest direction often begins with a truthful verse and continues through one quiet good deed.

blocks.label: CARRY FORWARD
blocks.text: Let hope, humility and service become a lasting legacy.

evidence.arabic: فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ يَحْيَىٰ وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُ زَوْجَهُ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ وَيَدْعُونَنَا رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا ۖ وَكَانُوا لَنَا خَاشِعِينَ
evidence.meaning: Allah granted Yaḥyā and describes their eagerness in good deeds, supplication in hope and fear, and humble devotion.

missions.question: The academy receives donated books. Mohsin says the class will now always get anything it asks for.

choices.text: Refuse the donation because future supplies are uncertain.
choices.feedback: Being grateful does not mean refusing a genuine gift. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Declare the donors must give more every week.
choices.feedback: A donation never creates a right to demand unlimited future gifts. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Express gratitude, use the books responsibly and avoid promises about the future.
choices.feedback: Gratitude includes using gifts well and speaking truthfully about what we cannot know.

missions.title: Hope with Respect

discover.text: ID: ZAK-M05 • Connected story 04 • Core evidence: Qur’an 19:4–5 • Supporting: 3:40

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Zakariyyā spoke sincerely of weakness, old age and a deeply personal hope. Children are not asked to disclose such circumstances. The lesson is respect for people’s dignity and trust in Allah.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I avoid jokes about somebody’s age, health, appearance or private family wishes?

evidence.meaning: Zakariyyā asked about the extraordinary gift in his old age, and the reply affirmed Allah’s will and power.

evidence.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا وَلَمْ أَكُنۢ بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا
evidence.meaning: He described his weakness and old age while remembering Allah’s mercy in his supplications.

evidence.arabic: وَإِنِّي خِفْتُ الْمَوَالِيَ مِن وَرَائِي وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنكَ وَلِيًّا
evidence.meaning: He expressed concern for what would follow him and asked Allah to grant a successor.

choices.text: Laugh loudly so the joke feels popular.
choices.feedback: Mockery can hurt and is not respectful. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Object kindly and thank the volunteer for their useful work.
choices.feedback: Respect includes defending people’s dignity without demanding personal explanations.

choices.text: Ask the volunteer invasive questions about private worries.

evidence.meaning: Allah granted Yaḥyā and describes their eagerness in good deeds, supplication in hope and fear, and humble devotion.

choices.feedback: Humiliating someone is not sound teaching. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

discover.text: ID: ZAK-M07 • Connected story 05 • Core evidence: Qur’an 19:7 • Supporting: 3:39

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Identify the Qur’anic glad tidings accurately and recognise them as a particular divine gift.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Read and listen to the approved full verse(s) at 19:7. The linked source library above provides working Arabic and meaning guidance. Approved muṣḥaf text must be pulled into the app from the authoritative verse store, never retyped from the story.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Allah gave Zakariyyā the special good news of Yaḥyā, a Prophet among the righteous. The account does not promise that every prayer for children will lead to the same worldly outcome.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Can I celebrate another person’s happiness without making promises I do not control?

evidence.arabic: فَنَادَتْهُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي فِي الْمِحْرَابِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكَ بِيَحْيَىٰ مُصَدِّقًا بِكَلِمَةٍ مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَسَيِّدًا وَحَصُورًا وَنَبِيًّا مِّنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
evidence.meaning: While he stood praying, angels brought the glad tidings of Yaḥyā, who would be among the righteous Prophets.

evidence.arabic: يَا زَكَرِيَّا إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ اسْمُهُ يَحْيَىٰ لَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُ مِن قَبْلُ سَمِيًّا
evidence.meaning: Allah gave Zakariyyā the glad tidings of a son named Yaḥyā.

missions.question: A friend receives welcome news and Akhlaq wants to announce, “Everything will now be perfect forever.”

choices.text: Ignore the news because hardships can exist.
choices.feedback: Positive news deserves thoughtful kindness. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Promise perfect outcomes to make everyone smile.
choices.feedback: Nobody has knowledge of a flawless future. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Congratulate kindly, thank Allah and offer real help without guaranteeing the future.
choices.feedback: Sincere good wishes and practical care are better than impossible guarantees.

missions.action: Congratulate a person appropriately, making no promise beyond your control.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Zakariyyā asked about the extraordinary gift, and the Qur’anic reply affirmed Allah’s power. Children should be free to ask a knowledgeable adult about difficult material while respecting people’s privacy.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY

evidence.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَامٌ وَقَدْ بَلَغَنِيَ الْكِبَرُ وَامْرَأَتِي عَاقِرٌ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ اللَّهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ
evidence.meaning: Zakariyyā asked about the extraordinary gift in his old age, and the reply affirmed Allah’s will and power.

evidence.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَامٌ وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا وَقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الْكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا
evidence.meaning: He wondered at receiving a son at an advanced age when his wife had not borne children.

evidence.arabic: قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ قَالَ رَبُّكَ هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ وَقَدْ خَلَقْتُكَ مِن قَبْلُ وَلَمْ تَكُ شَيْئًا

choices.text: Say the pupil is silly for not understanding immediately.

discover.label: LEARNING TARGET
discover.text: Describe the particular sign without reenacting it or stigmatising communication differences.

discover.label: DISCOVER — THE QUR’AN
discover.text: Read and listen to the approved full verse(s) at 19:10. The linked source library above provides working Arabic and meaning guidance. Approved muṣḥaf text must be pulled into the app from the authoritative verse store, never retyped from the story.

discover.label: UNDERSTAND — EXPLAINING THE GUIDANCE
discover.text: Allah gave Zakariyyā a unique sign concerning speech. In modern life, pupils should respect and support people who communicate through speech, signs, writing or communication aids.

discover.label: REFLECT — A QUESTION TO CARRY
discover.text: Do I give another person time to express themselves without rushing or teasing?

evidence.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ اجْعَل لِّي آيَةً ۖ قَالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ إِلَّا رَمْزًا ۗ وَاذْكُر رَّبَّكَ كَثِيرًا وَسَبِّحْ بِالْعَشِيِّ وَالْإِبْكَارِ
evidence.meaning: He was given a special sign of not speaking to people for three days except by gesture, with instruction to remember Allah often.

evidence.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ اجْعَل لِّي آيَةً ۖ قَالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَ لَيَالٍ سَوِيًّا
evidence.meaning: He requested a sign and was given the distinctive sign of not speaking for three nights while sound.

choices.text: Offer readable choices, allow time and ask what communication support helps.
choices.feedback: Respectful accessibility is a modern ethical application, not a reenactment of the divine sign.

choices.text: Treat the pupil’s communication method as a joke.
choices.feedback: Mockery creates exclusion rather than understanding. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

discover.text: Allah describes Zakariyyā’s household as eager to do good and turning to Him with hope, reverent fear and humility. These are virtues to practise, not levels a child can earn by collecting points.

evidence.arabic: فَخَرَجَ عَلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ مِنَ الْمِحْرَابِ فَأَوْحَىٰ إِلَيْهِمْ أَن سَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا
evidence.meaning: He signalled his people to glorify Allah morning and evening.

evidence.arabic: فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ يَحْيَىٰ وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُ زَوْجَهُ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ وَيَدْعُونَنَا رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا ۖ وَكَانُوا لَنَا خَاشِعِينَ
evidence.meaning: Allah granted Yaḥyā and describes their eagerness in good deeds, supplication in hope and fear, and humble devotion.

missions.question: After the exhibition, the group can either tidy shared materials or spend the whole time collecting praise.

choices.text: Leave the work and demand a public reward.
choices.feedback: Good work still needs to be completed after an event. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

choices.text: Help tidy, thank the team and reflect privately on a good habit to continue.
choices.feedback: Humility and useful action are better than making spiritual rankings or seeking applause.

choices.text: Compete to see whose faith score is highest.
choices.feedback: No classroom or app can assign an accurate rank to hearts. Review the verse and try again with supportive feedback.

missions.action: Perform one helpful action discreetly, if safe, and privately choose a habit to continue.

remember.label: REMEMBER — PRIVATE MUḤĀSABAH
remember.text: What is one quiet good deed I can practise without needing everyone to notice? Mark “Practised / Still learning / Skip” without public scores or proof uploads.

remember.label: VOCABULARY
remember.text: الْخَيْرَات — good deeds; خَاشِعِينَ — humbly devoted

review.arabic: فَتَقَبَّلَهَا رَبُّهَا بِقَبُولٍ حَسَنٍ وَأَنۢبَتَهَا نَبَاتًا حَسَنًا وَكَفَّلَهَا زَكَرِيَّا ۖ كُلَّمَا دَخَلَ عَلَيْهَا زَكَرِيَّا الْمِحْرَابَ وَجَدَ عِندَهَا رِزْقًا ۖ قَالَ يَا مَرْيَمُ أَنَّىٰ لَكِ هَٰذَا ۖ قَالَتْ هُوَ مِنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ ۖ إِنَّ اللَّهَ يَرْزُقُ مَن يَشَاءُ بِغَيْرِ حِسَابٍ
review.meaning: Allah accepted Maryam and placed her in Zakariyyā’s care. He found provision with her, and she attributed it to Allah.

review.arabic: هُنَالِكَ دَعَا زَكَرِيَّا رَبَّهُ ۖ قَالَ رَبِّ هَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنكَ ذُرِّيَّةً طَيِّبَةً ۖ إِنَّكَ سَمِيعُ الدُّعَاءِ
review.meaning: Zakariyyā asked his Lord for righteous offspring, acknowledging that Allah hears supplication.

review.arabic: فَنَادَتْهُ الْمَلَائِكَةُ وَهُوَ قَائِمٌ يُصَلِّي فِي الْمِحْرَابِ أَنَّ اللَّهَ يُبَشِّرُكَ بِيَحْيَىٰ مُصَدِّقًا بِكَلِمَةٍ مِّنَ اللَّهِ وَسَيِّدًا وَحَصُورًا وَنَبِيًّا مِّنَ الصَّالِحِينَ
review.meaning: While he stood praying, angels brought the glad tidings of Yaḥyā, who would be among the righteous Prophets.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَامٌ وَقَدْ بَلَغَنِيَ الْكِبَرُ وَامْرَأَتِي عَاقِرٌ ۖ قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ اللَّهُ يَفْعَلُ مَا يَشَاءُ
review.meaning: Zakariyyā asked about the extraordinary gift in his old age, and the reply affirmed Allah’s will and power.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ اجْعَل لِّي آيَةً ۖ قَالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَةَ أَيَّامٍ إِلَّا رَمْزًا ۗ وَاذْكُر رَّبَّكَ كَثِيرًا وَسَبِّحْ بِالْعَشِيِّ وَالْإِبْكَارِ
review.meaning: He was given a special sign of not speaking to people for three days except by gesture, with instruction to remember Allah often.
A reminder of Allah’s mercy toward His servant Zakariyyā.
He called on his Lord privately.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ إِنِّي وَهَنَ الْعَظْمُ مِنِّي وَاشْتَعَلَ الرَّأْسُ شَيْبًا وَلَمْ أَكُنۢ بِدُعَائِكَ رَبِّ شَقِيًّا
review.meaning: He described his weakness and old age while remembering Allah’s mercy in his supplications.

review.arabic: وَإِنِّي خِفْتُ الْمَوَالِيَ مِن وَرَائِي وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا فَهَبْ لِي مِن لَّدُنكَ وَلِيًّا
review.meaning: He expressed concern for what would follow him and asked Allah to grant a successor.

review.arabic: يَرِثُنِي وَيَرِثُ مِنْ آلِ يَعْقُوبَ ۖ وَاجْعَلْهُ رَبِّ رَضِيًّا
review.meaning: He prayed for a successor to continue the honoured legacy and to be pleasing to Allah.

review.arabic: يَا زَكَرِيَّا إِنَّا نُبَشِّرُكَ بِغُلَامٍ اسْمُهُ يَحْيَىٰ لَمْ نَجْعَل لَّهُ مِن قَبْلُ سَمِيًّا
review.meaning: Allah gave Zakariyyā the glad tidings of a son named Yaḥyā.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ أَنَّىٰ يَكُونُ لِي غُلَامٌ وَكَانَتِ امْرَأَتِي عَاقِرًا وَقَدْ بَلَغْتُ مِنَ الْكِبَرِ عِتِيًّا
review.meaning: He wondered at receiving a son at an advanced age when his wife had not borne children.

review.arabic: قَالَ كَذَٰلِكَ قَالَ رَبُّكَ هُوَ عَلَيَّ هَيِّنٌ وَقَدْ خَلَقْتُكَ مِن قَبْلُ وَلَمْ تَكُ شَيْئًا
review.meaning: The reply teaches Allah’s power: the One who created him before can grant this gift.

review.arabic: قَالَ رَبِّ اجْعَل لِّي آيَةً ۖ قَالَ آيَتُكَ أَلَّا تُكَلِّمَ النَّاسَ ثَلَاثَ لَيَالٍ سَوِيًّا
review.meaning: He requested a sign and was given the distinctive sign of not speaking for three nights while sound.

review.arabic: فَخَرَجَ عَلَىٰ قَوْمِهِ مِنَ الْمِحْرَابِ فَأَوْحَىٰ إِلَيْهِمْ أَن سَبِّحُوا بُكْرَةً وَعَشِيًّا
review.meaning: He signalled his people to glorify Allah morning and evening.

review.arabic: وَزَكَرِيَّا إِذْ نَادَىٰ رَبَّهُ رَبِّ لَا تَذَرْنِي فَرْدًا وَأَنتَ خَيْرُ الْوَارِثِينَ
review.meaning: Zakariyyā called upon Allah, asking not to be left without an heir, while affirming Allah as the best inheritor.

review.arabic: فَاسْتَجَبْنَا لَهُ وَوَهَبْنَا لَهُ يَحْيَىٰ وَأَصْلَحْنَا لَهُ زَوْجَهُ ۚ إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا يُسَارِعُونَ فِي الْخَيْرَاتِ وَيَدْعُونَنَا رَغَبًا وَرَهَبًا ۖ وَكَانُوا لَنَا خَاشِعِينَ
review.meaning: Allah granted Yaḥyā and describes their eagerness in good deeds, supplication in hope and fear, and humble devotion.

synthesis.text: What the Qur’an establishes

Zakariyyā (AS) is honoured among the righteous Prophets. The Qur’an describes Maryam placed in his care, an encounter concerning Allah’s provision, his private prayer and sincere concern for a righteous successor, the glad tidings of Yaḥyā, a unique sign relating to speech, and his call to remember Allah. Al-Anbiyāʾ 21:90 especially praises the household for eagerness in good deeds, calling on Allah with hope and reverent fear, and remaining humble. The manuscript adds no imagined stages of his life or unsourced events as though they were revelation.
Eight lasting lessons for children
TRUTHFUL REMEMBRANCE — Honor Prophets by checking Qur’anic sources and avoiding invented details.
PRIVATE DUʿĀʾ — Allah hears us when we call on Him sincerely; we can also seek trusted human support.
CARE AS A TRUST — Look after people and shared things with dignity, consideration and permission.
KIND QUESTIONS — Respectfully seek understanding and never mock age, disability or family circumstances.
GRATEFUL HOPE — Celebrate genuine blessings without claiming knowledge of future outcomes.
ACCESSIBLE COMMUNICATION — Give people space to express themselves and support different communication needs.
STEADY DHIKR — Remember Allah consistently and meaningfully rather than competing for public approval.
EAGER GOODNESS — Respond to blessings and responsibilities through humble, useful actions.
Carry forward — one-week family character practice
Day
Voluntary, child-friendly practice
Caregiver prompt
Learn Zakariyyā’s name and one correct Qur’anic reference.
What does the actual verse say?
Make a sincere personal duʿāʾ; discuss safe help-seeking if needed.
Who can help us when a worry needs adult support?
Improve one shared space for someone else.
Did we ask what would actually help?
Thank a helper or an older person without intrusive questions.
How can respect sound gentle and sincere?
Congratulate someone without promising the future.
Which kind words are ours to keep?
Try an accessible message and one optional morning/evening dhikr.
Can everyone understand and participate?
Do one helpful deed quietly and choose one habit to continue.
What could make goodness last into next week?
Final knowledge and character assessment
CHECK • Which Qur’anic passages give Zakariyyā’s principal story? ANSWER GUIDE • Āl ʿImrān 3:37–41; Maryam 19:2–11; al-Anbiyāʾ 21:89–90.
CHECK • Who was placed in Zakariyyā’s care? ANSWER GUIDE • Maryam, as reported in Qur’an 3:37.
CHECK • How does Maryam 19:3 describe his supplication? ANSWER GUIDE • He called on his Lord privately.
CHECK • What was the special good news given to him? ANSWER GUIDE • A son named Yaḥyā; see 19:7 and 3:39.
CHECK • What sign was given to Zakariyyā? ANSWER GUIDE • A particular period without speaking to people as normally, detailed in 19:10 and 3:41.
CHECK • What did he indicate to his people? ANSWER GUIDE • To glorify Allah morning and evening; 19:11.
CHECK • What qualities are praised in 21:90? ANSWER GUIDE • Eagerness in good deeds, supplication with hope and reverent fear, and humble devotion.
CHECK • Does his particular answered prayer promise the same result for every person? ANSWER GUIDE • No. The Qur’an reports a special divine gift; other outcomes and timing belong to Allah’s wisdom.
CHECK • How should a child react when private help or safety is needed? ANSWER GUIDE • Seek a trustworthy adult; duʿāʾ does not replace appropriate support.
CHECK • Can the app rank children’s faith from completed missions? ANSWER GUIDE • No. It tracks learning progress and voluntary practice, never spiritual rank.

CLOSING REFLECTION • Zakariyyā (AS) teaches me to honour true guidance, make sincere duʿāʾ, remember Allah, care for those entrusted to me and do good with humility. I do not need to perform goodness for an audience. I can carry one small responsible action into tomorrow.
